rejected.title: Women between the wars
card: Many women won the vote after the First World War: Germany in November 1918 and the United States in 1920. Britain gave it to women over 30 who met a property qualification in 1918, then to all women over 21 in 1928.
The war had put many women into paid work, and in the 1920s more women worked in offices, shops and factories. Most were paid less than men and were expected to leave work when they married.
Some young women, often called flappers, wore shorter skirts and short hair, and went out without a chaperone. This was a new freedom, but it was mostly seen among younger women in towns and cities.
Most women still faced limits. Many were expected to care for the home and children, and many jobs and professions were closed to them. Gains were real but uneven.
rejected.remember: Women gained votes and some new freedoms, but pay, jobs and home duties still held most of them back.

a.q: Which statement best describes women's lives in the 1920s?
opts: They gained new rights and freedoms, but limits remained
They gained full equality with men at work and at home
They kept the same lives as before the First World War
They lost the right to vote once men returned from war
a.why: Many women won the vote and had new freedoms in work and dress, but they were still paid less and expected to run the home. Full equality is wrong because the card shows many limits stayed in place.
a.clue: Think of both the gains and the limits.

b.q: Edith, a young typist in Manchester in 1926, wears her hair short and goes dancing with friends. She earns less than the men in her office and will be expected to quit if she marries. What does her case show?
opts: New freedoms existed alongside continuing limits
Women's pay had become equal to men's pay
Freedoms in dress had ended the limits on work
Only women who could vote had any new freedoms
b.why: Edith's short hair and dancing show new freedoms in dress and social life. Her lower pay and the expectation that she leave work on marriage show limits remained. The option claiming that dress freedoms ended work limits is tempting, but her own case disproves it.
b.clue: Look for what Edith gained and what still held her back.

problems.detail: Germany gave women the vote in November 1918 by decree of the new government. Women first voted in January 1919, so 'Germany in 1919' is misleading as the date the vote was given.

Britain's 1918 Act gave the vote only to women over 30 who met a property qualification (themselves or their husbands). 'Women over 30' overstates it, as many women over 30 still could not vote until 1928.
